title: Why adding 1 in C can make your number go negative
description:
In C, integers have a fixed number of bits, so arithmetic that goes past the type's range wraps around silently instead of raising an error. This Short shows INT_MAX plus one flipping straight to the most negative int, why the compiler won't warn you at runtime, and why a wider or unsigned type only moves the boundary instead of fixing it. Pulled from the C Mastery Path Level 1 lesson on variables, data types and operators.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Set a C int to its maximum value, then add one. No error. No bigger number. You get the most negative value the int can hold.
INT_MAX from limits dot h is about 2.1 billion. Print it and it's fine. Add one, and it wraps straight around to negative 2.1 billion. Silent. The program just keeps running.
Reaching for a long or an unsigned type buys you more headroom, but it doesn't fix this. It just moves the boundary further out.
So the rule: C will not catch this at runtime. If a value might get huge, pick a type with room to spare and check before you add.
